metaData.originalTitle: 2026 年了，AI Agent 为什么还是“Demo 很惊艳，上线就翻车”？
metaData.title: Why AI Agents Still Fail in Production in 2026: Great Demos, Terrible Deployments
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article delves into the five core contradictions behind why AI Agent products perform poorly after deployment despite impressive demos, identifying the root cause as the vast gap between sterile test environments and the real world, and proposes systematic solutions ranging from evaluation frameworks to expectation management.
metaData.summary: The article points out that from 2024 to 2026, AI Agent products have repeatedly fallen into the cycle of "impressive demos, failed deployments." The root cause is not simply insufficient model capability, but a convergence of multiple systemic contradictions. The author analyzes five dimensions: First, demos run in carefully curated "sterile environments," avoiding real-world noise and complexity. Second, evaluation systems are driven by "average scores," but user experience depends on the "worst moment" — one major failure can destroy user trust. Third, Agent capabilities are "chain-like," while evaluations are often "node-based," leading to cumulative error rates across multi-step chains far exceeding single-node performance. Fourth, there is a gap between model "capability" and product "product readiness," where the latter requires engineering design for input fault tolerance, edge case handling, and failure recovery. Fifth, the viral spread of demos inflates user expectations, causing the gap between the "average experience" and the "ceiling experience" to be perceived as a failure. Finally, the article proposes specific recommendations, including shifting from "average score-driven" to "worst-case-driven" evaluation, introducing "chain evaluation," strengthening productization design, and proactively managing expectations.

mainPoints.point: Demos run in "sterile environments," avoiding the complexity and noise of the real world.
mainPoints.explanation: Demo inputs, web pages, and interaction paths are carefully selected and rehearsed, while real user inputs are full of typos, complex page structures, ad interference, etc. These "noises" are bypassed rather than solved in demos, leading to a cliff-like drop in performance after deployment.

mainPoints.point: There is a fundamental misalignment between evaluation "average scores" and user experience "worst moments."
mainPoints.explanation: User trust in AI Agents is fragile — one egregious error can reset the trust built up over many previous successes. Current evaluation systems focus on average performance, but what truly determines user retention is how bad the worst case is, not how high the average score is.

mainPoints.point: The "chain-like" execution capability of Agents does not match the "node-based" evaluation logic.
mainPoints.explanation: Completing a task requires a multi-step chain. When the success rate of each step is multiplied, the overall success rate drops significantly. Evaluations often only focus on single-node capabilities, ignoring the dependencies between nodes and the risk of cumulative errors, leading to smooth demos but frequent failures in actual use.

mainPoints.point: There is a huge gap between model "capability" and product "product readiness."
mainPoints.explanation: Models can produce good results under ideal inputs, but product readiness requires engineering and design to address input fault tolerance, edge case handling, and failure recovery. Many teams prioritize models over productization, which is a major reason for deployment failures.

mainPoints.point: Demos inflate user expectations, causing the gap between the "ceiling" and the "average experience" to be perceived as a failure.
mainPoints.explanation: Demo virality raises user expectations to the ceiling level, while the actual experience is at the average level. This gap is amplified in user perception as a "failure." Effective expectation management, such as publishing "capability boundary descriptions," is key to narrowing this gap.

keyQuotes: The persuasiveness of a demo comes precisely from its avoidance of real-world complexity. It shows you "what an Agent can do under ideal conditions," not "what an Agent will encounter in actual use."
User trust in an Agent is the "most fragile equilibrium" — do ten things right, and trust slowly accumulates; mess up once, and trust vanishes instantly.
Agent capabilities are "chain-like," but our evaluations are often "node-based."
Capability can be improved through model training, but product readiness requires engineering design and product strategy to fill the gaps.
The gap from the ceiling to the average level is perceived by users as a "failure."
